posts.title: Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Commerce, Science, and Transportation, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, S. Rept. 119-160
posts.summary:
Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act
This bill directs the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to allow civil aircraft to operate at speeds above Mach 1 (i.e., supersonic) over land in the United States under certain conditions.
Specifically, the FAA must issue or revise regulations to allow for the operation of civil aircraft at speeds greater than Mach 1 in the national airspace system without a special authorization, so long as no sonic boom reaches the ground in the United States.
Current regulations prohibit civil aircraft from operating above Mach 1 speeds over land in the United States without a special flight authorization issued by the FAA.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Ted Budd (R-NC)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would require the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to allow civil aircraft to fly faster than the speed of sound, known as Mach 1, over land in the United States. Right now, flying that fast over land requires a special permission from the FAA.

Under the bill, the FAA must issue or change its rules so that civil aircraft can fly supersonic in the nation's airspace without that special permission. This applies only if no sonic boom reaches the ground in the United States.

posts.title: To expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
This bill expands the authority of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to provide information to certain persons (e.g., trademark or copyright owners) regarding suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
Under current law, if CBP suspects that merchandise is being imported in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws, it may request assistance from specified persons when determining whether the merchandise is imported in violation of these laws. To permit the party to conduct examination and testing, CBP must provide them with specified information that appears on the merchandise and its packaging and labels.
This bill (1) expands the definition of person to allow CBP to request assistance from any other appropriate party with an interest in the imported merchandise, and (2) expands the scope of information that CBP is authorized to share with others to include information on and images of packing materials and containers.
The bill allows CBP to request this assistance if it has a reasonable suspicion (currently, suspects) that the merchandise being imported is in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws.
Additionally, CBP may provide a person with nonpublic information about the imported merchandise that was generated by an online marketplace or similar market platform, express consignment operator, freight forwarder, or any other entity that plays a role in the sale, importation, or facilitation of the merchandise into the United States and has been provided to, shared with, or obtained by CBP. CBP must provide the person with notification of the transmitted information.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.committee: Finance Committee, Ways and Means Committee
posts.meta: Finance Committee, Ways and Means Committee · Rep. Blake Moore (R-UT)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill gives U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) more power to get outside help when it suspects that imported goods infringe on trademarks or copyrights. Under current law, CBP can ask certain people, such as trademark or copyright owners, to help decide whether goods are illegal copies, and it can share specified label and packaging information so they can examine and test the goods. The bill widens both parts of that system.

First, it lets CBP ask for help from any other appropriate party with an interest in the imported goods, not just the specified groups covered now. Second, it expands the information CBP can share to include information about and images of packing materials and containers, not only what appears on the goods and their labels.

The bill also lowers the threshold for asking for help. Right now CBP must suspect a violation. Under the bill, it may act if it has a reasonable suspicion that the goods violate certain trademark and copyright laws.

In addition, CBP may give a person nonpublic information about the imported goods that was generated by an online marketplace or similar platform, an express consignment operator, a freight forwarder, or any other entity involved in selling, importing, or moving the goods into the United States. That information must have been provided to, shared with, or obtained by CBP. When CBP shares it, it must notify the person that the information was sent.

posts.title: Disaster Communications Coordination and Preparedness Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Commerce, Science, and Transportation, without amendment, S. Rept. 119-159
posts.summary:
Disaster Communications Coordination and Preparedness Act
This bill directs the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to assess its procedures for disasters and emergencies affecting communications service and consider measures to improve coordination with officials and service providers during such events.
Specifically, the FCC must review and update, as appropriate, its procedures for notifying communications service providers about activations and deactivations of the Disaster Information Reporting System (DIRS). (DIRS is activated during severe weather and other events to enable providers to report outages and other service issues.)
Further, the FCC must provide plain-language resources for state, local, tribal, and territorial officials on federal communications and emergency coordination mechanisms available during disasters and emergencies. To the extent practicable, these materials must include information on DIRS, the Mandatory Disaster Response Initiative (MDRI), and services that may be available to support public safety communications during such events, among other topics. (MDRI requires cell service providers to coordinate and share resources during emergencies.)
Finally, the FCC must consider enhancing its functions related to (1) informing state, local, tribal, and territorial officials of the status of communications services during disasters and emergencies; and (2) facilitating coordination between these officials and communications providers before, during, and after such events.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-MT)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill asks the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to look at how it handles communications during disasters and emergencies, and to find ways to work better with local officials and phone and internet companies when those events happen.

First, the FCC must review and, where appropriate, update how it tells communications companies when the Disaster Information Reporting System (DIRS) is turned on or off. DIRS is switched on during severe weather and similar events so that providers can report outages and other service problems.

Second, the FCC must put together plain-language materials for state, local, tribal, and territorial officials explaining the federal communications and emergency coordination tools available during disasters. Where practical, these materials must cover DIRS, the Mandatory Disaster Response Initiative (MDRI), and services that may help support public safety communications during these events, along with other topics. MDRI requires cell service providers to coordinate and share resources during emergencies.

Third, the FCC must consider ways to expand its work in two areas: keeping state, local, tribal, and territorial officials informed about the status of communications services during disasters and emergencies, and helping those officials and communications providers coordinate before, during, and after such events.

posts.title: NASA Transition Authorization Act of 2025
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Commerce, Science, and Transportation, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, S. Rept. 119-156
posts.summary:
NASA Transition Authorization Act of 2025
This bill reauthorizes through FY2025 the programs and activities of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). The bill also revises certain existing NASA programs and establishes new programs related to space exploration, research, and technology.
For example, the bill directs NASA to continue its efforts to support crewed lunar landings and Mars explorations, including through partnerships with the private sector (i.e., the Moon to Mars and Artemis programs).
The bill also requires NASA to maintain the capability for a continuous human presence in low-Earth orbit until and beyond the retirement of the International Space Station (ISS). NASA may solicit proposals for the development of a commercial space station in low-Earth orbit. When such a station is ready, NASA must initiate an orderly transition of operations from the ISS to the commercial station. NASA must also develop a de-orbit vehicle for the eventual retirement of the ISS. (Low-Earth orbit encompasses orbits at an altitude of 1,200 miles or less.)
In addition, NASA is authorized to develop an architecture for lunar communications and navigation, and must develop a strategy to implement a standardized lunar time to support operations and infrastructure on and around the moon.
NASA must also continue to conduct research relating to advanced air mobility, unmanned aircraft systems (i.e., drones), and hypersonic technologies.
Finally, the bill requires the Government Accountability Office to report on fire and emergency services at NASA launch and reentry facilities.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill extends NASA's existing programs and activities through fiscal year 2025, and it also changes some current programs and creates new ones focused on space exploration, research, and technology. It directs NASA to keep working toward crewed landings on the Moon and exploration of Mars, including through partnerships with private companies. These efforts fall under the Moon to Mars and Artemis programs.

The bill requires NASA to keep a continuous human presence in low-Earth orbit, meaning orbits at an altitude of 1,200 miles or less, until and beyond the retirement of the International Space Station (ISS). NASA may ask companies to propose a commercial space station in low-Earth orbit. Once that station is ready, NASA must begin an orderly move of operations from the ISS to it. NASA must also develop a de-orbit vehicle, a spacecraft that would bring the ISS down when it is eventually retired.

The bill also allows NASA to design a system for communications and navigation on the Moon. It requires NASA to develop a plan for a standard lunar time to support activities on and around the Moon.

In addition, NASA must keep researching advanced air mobility, unmanned aircraft systems (drones), and hypersonic technologies.

Finally, the Government Accountability Office must report on fire and emergency services at NASA's launch and reentry facilities.

posts.title: SAFEGUARDS Act of 2025
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Commerce, Science, and Transportation, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, S. Rept. 119-157
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Jerry Moran (R-KS)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)
posts.summary:
Spending Aviation Fees for Equipment, Guaranteeing Upgraded and Advanced Risk Detection and Safety Act of 2025 or the SAFEGUARDS Act of 2025
This bill allocates additional funding for the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) for aviation security, including checked baggage explosives detection equipment and security checkpoint technology.
As background, TSA collects passenger civil aviation security service fees (often referred to as the 9/11 security fee or passenger security fee) on air carrier passengers originating at airports in the United States. In general, these fees are deposited into the Department of the Treasury general fund and applied towards debt reduction. A portion of these fees are allocated to TSA for aviation security.
The bill requires that the first $500 million collected in each fiscal year from passenger security fees be deposited into the Aviation Security Capital Fund. This is an increase from the currently required $250 million. This fund provides for the costs associated with acquiring and installing in-line baggage screening systems (i.e., systems that use a conveyor belt infrastructure to automatically screen, sort, and track baggage) to accommodate checked baggage explosives detection equipment and for certain other airport security improvements.
The bill also requires that the next $250 million collected in each fiscal year from passenger security fees be deposited into a new Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund for the costs associated with acquiring, deploying, and sustaining aviation security checkpoint and exit lane technology. TSA may use these funds retroactively for projects implemented on or after January 1, 2023.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate

aiSummaries.text:
The SAFEGUARDS Act of 2025 is meant to pay for better airport security equipment. It adds money for the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) to buy and maintain checked-baggage explosives detection machines and technology used at security checkpoints.

Right now, TSA collects a passenger security fee (often called the 9/11 security fee) from air travelers departing from U.S. airports. Most of that money goes into the Treasury's general fund and is used to reduce the federal debt, and only part of it is given to TSA for aviation security.

Under the bill, the first $500 million collected each fiscal year from these fees would go into an Aviation Security Capital Fund. That is up from the $250 million currently required. This fund pays for installing in-line baggage screening systems, which use conveyor belts to automatically screen, sort, and track checked bags, and for certain other airport security upgrades.

The next $250 million collected each year would go into a new Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund. This money would cover buying, setting up, and keeping in working order the technology used at security checkpoints and exit lanes. TSA could also use this fund for projects started on or after January 1, 2023.

posts.summary:
Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026
This bill requires the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to increase the amounts payable for wartime disability compensation, additional compensation for dependents, the clothing allowance for certain disabled veterans, and dependency and indemnity compensation for surviving spouses and children. Specifically, the VA must increase the amounts by the same percentage as the cost-of-living increase in benefits for Social Security recipients that is effective on December 1, 2026. The VA is authorized to make a similar adjustment to the rates of disability compensation payable to persons who have not received compensation for service-connected disability or death.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House

aiSummaries.text:
This bill requires the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to raise several benefit payments for veterans and their families. The payments covered are wartime disability compensation, extra compensation for dependents, the clothing allowance for certain disabled veterans, and dependency and indemnity compensation for surviving spouses and children.

The increase is set by the same percentage as the cost-of-living increase for Social Security recipients that takes effect on December 1, 2026. In other words, the veterans' payments rise by that same percentage.

The VA must publish the new, higher payment amounts in the Federal Register, the official government publication where such notices appear.

The VA is also allowed, though not required, to make a similar adjustment to disability compensation rates for people who have not received compensation for a service-connected disability or death.

posts.title: America's National Churchill Museum National Historic Landmark Act
posts.label: 📌 Presented to President
posts.summary:
America's National Churchill Museum National Historic Landmark Act
This bill designates the America’s National Churchill Museum, including the Winston Churchill Memorial, located at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, as the America’s National Churchill Museum National Historic Landmark. (Former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill gave a speech titled The Sinews of Peace, also widely known as the Iron Curtain Speech, at the college in 1946.)
The bill permits the Department of the Interior to enter into cooperative agreements with public and private entities for the purposes of protecting historic resources at the landmark and providing educational and interpretive facilities for the public. Interior may provide technical and financial assistance to partner entities.
The bill also directs Interior to conduct a special resource study to evaluate the national significance of the landmark and to determine the suitability and feasibility of designating it as a unit of the National Park System. The study must consider alternatives to that designation for the preservation, protection, and interpretation of the landmark, and must include cost estimates associated with identified alternatives.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Natural Resources Committee · Rep. Robert Onder (R-MO)
posts.whatsNext: President has 10 days (Sundays excepted): sign, veto, or it becomes law unsigned (pocket veto if adjournment prevents return)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would designate the America's National Churchill Museum, including the Winston Churchill Memorial at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, as the America's National Churchill Museum National Historic Landmark. The college is the place where former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill gave his 1946 speech "The Sinews of Peace," also widely known as the Iron Curtain Speech.

The bill allows the Department of the Interior to make cooperative agreements with public and private groups. These agreements would aim to protect the historic features of the landmark and to provide educational and interpretive facilities for the public. Interior may also give technical and financial help to these partner groups.

The bill also requires Interior to carry out a special resource study. This study would evaluate how nationally important the landmark is and whether it would be suitable and feasible to make it a unit of the National Park System. The study must look at other options for preserving, protecting, and explaining the landmark, and it must include cost estimates for those options.

posts.title: Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.summary:
Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act
This bill expedites the process of reviewing certain uncontested permits and licenses for nuclear power plants (e.g., construction permits and operating licenses) by removing a requirement for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to hold a public hearing at the end of the process. The bill applies to the licenses and permits if a hearing has not been requested by a person whose interest may be affected. The bill also directs the NRC to use informal adjudicatory procedures if such a hearing is held.
Additionally, the bill directs the NRC to hold an adjudicatory hearing regarding the licensing of the construction and operation of a uranium enrichment facility only if the person whose interest may be affected by such construction and operation has requested the hearing.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. H. Griffith (R-VA)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill speeds up how the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approves certain nuclear power plant permits and licenses, such as those for building a plant or running one. Normally the NRC holds a public hearing at the end of the review. Under this bill, that final hearing is no longer required for permits and licenses that no one has asked to contest, meaning no person whose interests could be affected has requested a hearing. When a hearing is held, the NRC must use informal procedures rather than formal ones.

The bill also changes the rules for uranium enrichment facilities, which are plants that process uranium. For these, the NRC holds an adjudicatory hearing on the building and operation of the facility only if a person whose interests may be affected by it has asked for one.

posts.title: NRC Staff Pay Alignment Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.summary:
The following analysis is based on draft bill text that was made available by the House of Representatives and may differ from the bill text as introduced.
NRC Staff Pay Alignment Act
This bill allows the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to increase the annual compensation of a career appointee. Specifically, NRC may set such compensation at a rate that is up to 10% over the maximum annual rate of basic pay for a Senior Executive Service position within the NRC. This authority applies regardless of when the career appointee was appointed.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. Robert Menendez (D-NJ)

aiSummaries.text: This bill would let the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) raise the yearly pay of one of its career employees. The NRC could set that pay up to 10% above the highest standard yearly base pay for a Senior Executive Service job at the agency. This applies no matter when the career employee was hired.

posts.title: United States Commission on International Religious Freedom Reauthorization Act of 2026
posts.label: 📜✍️ Signed by Pres. Trump
posts.summary:
United States Commission on International Religious Freedom Reauthorization Act of 2026
This bill reauthorizes the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom through 2028. The commission is an independent federal commission tasked with monitoring international religious freedom conditions, reviewing U.S. government policy, and making policy recommendations. (Under current law, the commission is authorized through FY2026.)

aiSummaries.text: This bill extends the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom through 2028. The commission is an independent federal body that keeps track of how religious freedom is treated around the world, reviews U.S. government policy on the issue, and offers policy recommendations. Under current law, its authority runs only through fiscal year 2026, so this bill keeps it going beyond that point.

posts.title: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
posts.label: 📜✍️ Signed by Pres. Trump
posts.summary:
Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
This bill reauthorizes through FY2031 and revises programs that support research and development of drugs and other therapies to address amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (also known as ALS or Lou Gehrig's disease) and other neurodegenerative diseases.
The bill reauthorizes
grants from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for scientific research on investigational drugs to prevent or treat ALS for individuals not otherwise eligible for clinical trials,
grants from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for research and development of therapies to prevent and treat ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases, and
a Public-Private Partnership including the FDA and NIH that supports development and regulatory review of treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.
Also, the NIH, in considering renewal of its grants, must assess available information on the safety and efficacy of the investigational drugs. It must also require grantees to promptly report serious and unexpected adverse events associated with their investigational drugs.
Additionally, the FDA must publish a plan describing actions it will take over a five-year period to foster development of safe and effective drugs, and facilitate access to investigational drugs, that treat ALS and other rare neurodegenerative diseases. The FDA must also publish a report describing the actions it has taken under the plan.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. Mike Quigley (D-IL)
posts.whatsNext: Takes effect (on enactment unless the text sets other dates)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill extends several federal programs through fiscal year 2031 that fund research and development of drugs and other treatments for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, also called Lou Gehrig's disease) and other brain-related diseases that get worse over time.

Three programs are renewed. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) can keep giving grants for research on experimental drugs to prevent or treat ALS for people who can't otherwise join clinical trials. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) can keep giving grants to develop therapies for ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases. A public-private partnership involving the FDA and NIH can also keep supporting the development and regulatory review of treatments for these diseases.

The bill adds some safety requirements. When the NIH decides whether to renew one of these grants, it must review the available information on how safe and effective the experimental drug is. It must also require grant recipients to report serious and unexpected side effects promptly.

The FDA must publish a five-year plan describing what it will do to encourage the development of safe and effective drugs for ALS and other rare neurodegenerative diseases, and to make experimental drugs easier to access. Afterward, it must publish a report on the actions it has taken under that plan.
